questions.search_text:
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme that catalyses the conversion of pyruvate to lactate. Different organisms express LDH variants adapted to their thermal environment.

Scientists compared LDH from an Antarctic fish and a temperate fish. They measured relative enzyme activity across a range of temperatures.

LDH has a three-dimensional structure including:
- an active site, where substrate binds
- a hydrophobic core, stabilising the folded enzyme
- surface regions that interact with solvent and other molecules

Researchers modeled the structural effects of mutations in cold-adapted and warm-adapted LDH.

Examples include:
- replacing a buried hydrophobic residue with a charged one
- adding flexible residues (e.g., glycine)
- altering packing around the active site

A single amino-acid substitution can be sufficient to alter an enzyme's thermal properties.

A. TRUE
B. FALSE

questions.search_text:
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme that catalyses the conversion of pyruvate to lactate. Different organisms express LDH variants adapted to their thermal environment.

Scientists compared LDH from an Antarctic fish and a temperate fish. They measured relative enzyme activity across a range of temperatures.

Scientists investigated two inhibitors of LDH:

Vmax is the maximum rate of reaction an enzyme can achieve.
Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half Vmax.
Competitive inhibitors usually increase the apparent Km, while non-competitive inhibitors usually reduce Vmax.

Some inhibitors bind at a site other than the active site. These are called allosteric inhibitors.
Allosteric inhibitors may change the enzyme's shape and reduce its activity.

Inhibitor A causes the reaction curve to shift right, indicating a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach the same rate.

A. TRUE
B. FALSE
